report title and Executive Summary heading with surrounding blank lines

spans.assertion: the study estimated adjusted risk differences and odds ratios for red cards by skin tone by fitting linear probability models and logistic regression with player-clustered standard errors
the primary estimand, adjusted risk difference, was 0.202 percentage points (95% CI -0.091 to 0.495; p=0.177)
the secondary estimand, adjusted odds ratio, was 1.160 (95% CI 0.923 to 1.458; p=0.203)
the hypothesis of referee discrimination is not supported because the CIs include zero and p-values exceed the 0.05 threshold
the adjusted risk difference point estimate was 0.202pp with 95% CI [-0.091,0.495]pp, SE 0.150pp (clustered at player level), t=1.350, p=0.1769
dark-skinned players (rating ≥0.75) have an estimated 0.20pp higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players (rating ≤0.25) after adjustment
this estimated difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional significance levels
the adjusted odds ratio point estimate was 1.160, 95% CI [0.923,1.458], log-odds coefficient 0.1487, SE 0.1166 (clustered at player level), z=1.275, p=0.2025
the odds of a red card are 1.16 times higher for dark-skinned than light-skinned players
this odds-ratio estimate is not statistically significant since the CI includes 1.0

spans.note: Section 3 heading and Unit of Analysis subheading

spans.assertion: the analysis used the player-referee dyad as its unit of analysis
the analytic frame comprised 93,531 dyads from 1,141 players and 2,753 referees
each observation was defined as the cumulative encounters between one specific player and one specific referee across the season
red cards were rare: 1,150 dyads (1.23%) had at least one
light skin was defined as average rater score ≤0.25
the light-skin group comprised 84,050 dyads (89.9%)
dark skin was defined as average rater score ≥0.75
the dark-skin group comprised 9,481 dyads (10.1%)
skin tone was rated independently by two blind raters on a 5-point scale
inter-rater reliability was excellent (Pearson r=0.92, Spearman ρ=0.86)
the primary analysis compared only the light/dark extremes, excluding medium skin tones (0.25<score<0.75) to maximize contrast
the outcome was defined as any red card received in the dyad, coded as a binary indicator
the fully-adjusted Model 5 (primary specification) controlled for a specific set of covariates
the model adjusted for number of games in the dyad (median=1, max=47)
the model adjusted for player position using 12 categories
the model adjusted for player height in cm
35 missing height values were median-imputed
the model adjusted for player weight in kg
590 missing weight values were median-imputed
the model adjusted for yellow cards received, as a proxy for aggressive play style
the model adjusted for goals scored, as a proxy for offensive involvement
the model adjusted for league country (England, Germany, France, Spain)
five models were fit with progressively added covariate adjustment

across the five model specifications the risk difference and p-value were: unadjusted 0.193pp/0.180; +games 0.240pp/0.099; +player characteristics 0.224pp/0.123; +behavior 0.232pp/0.103; full model 0.202pp/0.177
all five models show positive point estimates but none reach significance at α=0.05

spans.note: blank and Standard Errors and Clustering subheading

spans.assertion: standard errors were clustered at the player level as the conservative choice to account for non-independence of dyads
on average each player appears in 82 dyads and each referee in 34 dyads, and skin tone is a player-level characteristic
a sensitivity analysis using referee-level clustering instead of player-level clustering produced nearly identical results (RD=0.202pp, 95% CI -0.048 to 0.452, p=0.113)

spans.note: blank and Exclusions and Missing Data subheading

spans.assertion: the original dataset contained 146,028 dyads
dyads with missing skin ratings were excluded
124,621 dyads (85.3%) were retained after this exclusion, with 21,407 excluded because the players lacked photos
the sample was restricted to light vs. dark skin tone, excluding medium tones
100,527 dyads remained after this restriction, with 24,094 excluded as medium skin tone
dyads missing player position data were excluded because position was required for adjustment
the final analysis sample was 93,531 dyads (64.1% of the original), with 6,996 excluded for missing position
missing height (N=35) and weight (N=590) values were median-imputed to retain sample size
skin tone was averaged across the two raters then dichotomized into ≤0.25 vs. ≥0.75 categories
red cards were dichotomized to any vs. none, collapsing the original 0-2 range
categorical variables (position, league country) were dummy-coded with reference categories
a linear probability model was fit via OLS with HC3 and cluster-robust standard errors as the primary method, chosen for interpretable risk differences
logistic regression (GLM, binomial family) with cluster-robust standard errors was fit as a secondary method to estimate odds ratios

spans.note: divider and Section 4 heading with surrounding blanks

spans.assertion: the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported at α=0.05
the 0.202pp risk difference corresponds to an absolute increase from a 1.21% light-skin baseline to a 1.41% dark-skin predicted rate, a ~16% relative increase
despite the direction matching the hypothesis, the effect magnitude is judged small
the 95% CI for the risk difference is wide (-0.09 to +0.50pp) and includes zero, indicating substantial uncertainty and that no effect or a protective effect cannot be ruled out
p=0.177 exceeds the pre-specified α=0.05 threshold, failing to reject the null hypothesis
the odds ratio CI also includes 1.0 (p=0.203)
all five model specifications show positive point estimates but none achieve significance
the estimate is relatively stable across adjustment strategies (range 0.19-0.24pp)
results are described as robust across sensitivity analyses
treating skin tone continuously yielded RD=0.24pp per unit increase, p=0.14
using referee-level clustering instead of player-level clustering yielded RD=0.20pp, p=0.11
the evidence is described as suggestive but inconclusive, with the consistent positive direction and a near-significant Model 2 result (p=0.099) hinting at a possible small effect
the study may be underpowered to detect small effects given the imbalanced group sizes (~90% light vs. ~10% dark)

spans.note: blank and 'Measurement of Skin Tone' subheading

spans.assertion: skin tone was rated from static photos rather than in-game appearance, which may introduce measurement error via lighting, photo quality, and rater subjectivity

spans.note: interpretive claim that any misclassification is non-differential and biases toward the null
reassurance restating inter-rater reliability and blind-rater design as mitigating the measurement limitation
blank and 'Selection Bias from Missing Data' subheading

spans.assertion: 36% of dyads were excluded overall (21% missing photos, 7% missing position, 8% medium skin tone)
the 6,996 dyads excluded for missing position had a similar red card rate (1.34% vs. 1.23%) to the analysis sample, suggesting minimal selection bias
missing data appeared to be missing at random
excluding medium skin tones was a deliberate conservative choice to maximize contrast, at the cost of reduced generalizability

hypothetical statement about aggression/refereeing context confounding the estimate

spans.assertion: adding yellow cards to the model barely changed the estimate (Model 3: 0.22pp → Model 4: 0.23pp), suggesting it is not a strong mediator or confounder

spans.note: blank and 'Unit of Analysis and Dependence Structure' subheading

spans.assertion: the player-referee dyad is not an independent unit; each player appears in ~82 dyads and each referee in ~34
two-way clustering by player and referee would have been the ideal approach but was judged computationally complex, so one-way clustering was used instead
clustering standard errors at the player level was the conservative choice, and referee-level clustering produced similar results

spans.note: hypothetical statement that the effect may vary by league, position, or referee

spans.assertion: by league, Germany shows RD=+0.82pp and Spain shows RD=-0.42pp, an opposite-direction result
by position, goalkeepers show RD=+0.11pp versus +0.41pp for center backs

spans.note: interpretive note that the average effect may mask heterogeneity

spans.assertion: the primary model adjusted for league and position, and exploratory (non-primary) interaction analyses were run to examine heterogeneity

spans.note: background on rare-event bias and LPM-vs-logistic tradeoffs

spans.assertion: LPM predicted probabilities remained within [0,1] in this application, and the logistic OR (1.16) was non-significant, consistent with the LPM result
both the LPM risk difference and the logistic odds ratio were reported for robustness

spans.note: intro clause framing the underpowering limitation

spans.assertion: the baseline red card rate is low (1.2%)
the exposure groups are imbalanced (90% light vs. 10% dark)
the data have a clustered structure
a t-statistic of 1.35 suggests roughly 50-60% post-hoc power, and a larger or more balanced sample would improve precision

spans.note: caveat that non-significance does not prove no effect
general limitation that observational design precludes causal claims
hypothetical alternative explanations for a significant finding

spans.assertion: the model adjusted for measurable confounders
an exploratory analysis of referee implicit bias (IAT scores) found no significant interaction with skin tone (p=0.36)

spans.note: divider, Section 6 heading, and 'Continuous Skin Tone' subheading

spans.assertion: treating skin tone as continuous yielded RD=0.24pp per unit (95% CI -0.08 to 0.57, p=0.14), consistent with the primary analysis and suggestive of a linear dose-response

spans.note: blank and 'Alternative Skin Tone Definition' subheading

spans.assertion: using a less stringent skin tone split (light <0.5 vs. dark >0.5) yielded nearly identical results (RD=0.20pp, p=0.18), confirming robustness to the categorization choice

spans.note: blank and 'Referee Implicit Bias Interaction' subheading

spans.assertion: an exploratory test of whether referee-country implicit bias (IAT) moderates the skin tone effect found no significant interaction (p=0.36)
implicit bias had a direct positive association with red cards overall (p=0.03), i.e. a main effect rather than a differential-by-skin-tone effect
effect estimates varied by league (Germany +0.82pp, England +0.27pp, Spain -0.42pp, France -0.47pp)

spans.note: divider, Section 7 heading, and 'Key Assumptions' subheading

spans.assertion: the LPM assumed a linear relationship between covariates and probability
predicted probabilities remained within [0,1], supporting that the linearity assumption approximately holds
the analysis assumed no unmeasured confounding, i.e. no omitted variables jointly predict skin tone and red cards
the analysis assumed player-level clustering correctly captures the dependence structure
the analysis assumed dyads within a player are independent conditional on covariates
the analysis assumed missing photos and positions are missing at random conditional on observed variables
variance inflation factors for key covariates were below 2, indicating no problematic multicollinearity
the maximum games per dyad was 47, a few high-leverage observations, but robust SEs mitigate their influence
the logistic model converged without warnings and predicted probabilities align with observed rates

spans.note: divider and Section 8 heading with surrounding blanks

spans.assertion: all analyses were conducted in Python 3.11 using pandas, statsmodels, scipy, numpy, and matplotlib
complete analysis code was provided in final_analysis.py, executable to reproduce all results
a random seed was not required because no simulation or bootstrap procedure was used
all data came from the provided soccer.csv file

spans.note: divider and Final Determination heading with surrounding blanks

spans.assertion: the overall determination is that the hypothesis is not supported, since the 95% CI includes zero, p=0.177 exceeds the significance threshold, and the study may lack adequate power
